input.topic: Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia: Autosomal Dominant Inheritance

expected.question_text: A 28-year-old male presents to the clinic for a routine physical examination. He has no complaints and mentions he is excited because his wife is pregnant with a boy. His past medical history is positive for mild hypercalcemia. He hands you the pedigree (seen in the exhibit) while informing you that several family members have the same condition. On physical examination, he appears well-developed and healthy with no abnormal findings. Laboratory examination reveals: | Serum calcium | 10.9 mg/dL | 8.6-10.0 mg/dL | |---|---|---| | N-terminal serum parathyroid hormone concentration | 72 pg/mL | 14-72 pg/mL | His fractional excretion of urinary calcium is less than 1%. Given the pedigree, what is the likelihood that his newborn son will have the disease?
expected.explanation_footer:
In autosomal dominant (AD) inheritance, only one dominant allele on an autosome (nonsex chromosome) is required for the trait or disorder to be passed to the next generation. The most common genotype of individuals with autosomal dominant diseases is heterozygous. When a heterozygous affected person mates with a homozygous unaffected person, there is a one in two (50%) chance that each of their offspring will be affected. Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) is characterized by mild elevations in both serum calcium and parathyroid hormone (PTH) with a urinary calcium clearance less than 0.01. FHH is due to an autosomal dominant mutation in the calcium-sensing receptor (CASR) causing a relative resistance to calcium. The CASR is a membrane-bound G protein-coupled receptor that has a calcium binding (sensing) site on its extracellular side. This receptor is found in abundance in the chief cells of the parathyroid glands and the cells lining the kidney tubules, where it plays a key role in calcium homeostasis. When the extracellular calcium concentration is high, large amounts of calcium ions bind to the receptor. This calcium-receptor binding activates intracellular signaling pathways that inhibit the secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH) from the parathyroid glands and block the reabsorption of calcium from the kidney, preventing processes that would further increase the serum calcium level. Conversely, when the extracellular calcium concentration is low, less calcium is bound to the receptor, which stimulates the secretion of PTH and increases the reabsorption of calcium from the kidney. Remember, the major function of PTH, secreted by the chief cells of the parathyroid gland, is to increase the amount of calcium in the blood. Normally, the CASR is very sensitive to changes in serum calcium. However, in FHH, an autosomal dominant inactivating (loss of function) mutation causes the receptor to become less sensitive to calcium. Therefore, a higher-than-normal calcium concentration is required for calcium-receptor binding to inhibit PTH secretion and increase urinary calcium excretion. This is why patients with FHH have mild hypercalcemia (11-12 mg/dL range) with a mildly elevated PTH and hypocalciuria. FHH does not cause disease or dysfunction, but is an important diagnosis to make, so that the patient is not misdiagnosed with primary hyperparathyroidism and subjected to unnecessary surgical removal of the parathyroid glands. Pedigrees are high-yield material, and you must know how to recognize an autosomal dominant (AD) pattern of inheritance on a pedigree. The following clues will allow you do so quickly and easily. There will be at least one affected person in every generation. The phenotype manifests in both males and females with a relatively equal frequency because it is autosomal. Every affected individual in the pedigree has an either an affected mom or dad. (vertical transmission) Unaffected individuals do not produce affected children. Since the mutation occurs on autosomal (nonsex) chromosomes, the sex of the parent and the child is irrelevant in the transmission of the trait. Humans have two alleles per gene each located at corresponding loci (the position of a gene on a chromosome) on homologous chromosomes, referred to as the gene locus. An allele is a version of a gene that codes for a particular phenotype (observable characteristic). One allele is inherited from a person's mom and the other allele from a person's dad. Individuals who have two identical alleles at a given gene locus are homozygous. Those who have two different alleles at a given gene locus are heterozygous. In autosomal dominant diseases, the mutated gene is a dominant allele located on one of the autosomal (nonsex) chromosomes. Dominant means that at a given gene locus, only one mutant allele is required to express the disease phenotype. In contrast, in autosomal recessive disorders, two copies of the mutant allele for a given gene are required for the disease to manifest. The Punnett square is a useful tool for answering questions about the likelihood of the offspring having the trait or disease. In Punnett square, capital letters represent dominant alleles. Lowercase letters represent recessive alleles. On the top of the squares are both alleles from the mother. On the side of the squares are both alleles from the father. The four boxes in the middle represent the four different genetic possibilities. Each of the four genetic possibilities is equally likely to occur in each offspring. The yellow highlighted boxes indicate the individuals with the trait or disorder. https://d2vrujxrqm3l5p.cloudfront.net/08e310a1-7289-4716-b0cd-c46ffebc35b6.jpg AD diseases usually manifest in the heterozygous state (with one dominant mutant mutant allele and one normal allele). Therefore, we can see from the Punnett square that when an affected person mates with an unaffected person, each offspring has a one in two (50% chance) of inheriting the mutant allele and being affected by the disease. Similarly, each individual has a one in two (50%) chance of inheriting the normal allele and being unaffected. 0% (choice A) is only possible if neither parents has the mutant allele and therefore neither parent has the disease. In families with AD diseases, only those offspring with two unaffected parents have a 0% chance of being affected. 25% (choice B) is not possible. In autosomal dominant inheritance, there is no cross between two parents that would result in a likelihood of 25% of the offspring inheriting the mutant allele and being affected. This would only be possible with an autosomal recessive mutation where both parents were heterozygous. In such a situation, two abnormal genes are needed to cause the disease and the chance of an offspring with two “lowercase h’s” from two heterozygous parents would be 25%. An example of an autosomal recessive mutation is cystic fibrosis. 75% (choice D) is only possible if both parents are affected by the disease. https://d2vrujxrqm3l5p.cloudfront.net/62cfc565-6f28-4bb2-a121-671984d25546.jpg If both parents are heterozygous affected (have one copy of the dominant mutant allele) then their child has a three in four (75%) chance of having the disease. As you can see from the Punnett square, in every pregnancy, each offspring has a 50% chance of being heterozygous affected (Hh), a 25% chance of being homozygous affected (HH), and a 25% chance of being homozygous for the normal allele (hh) and not at all affected. All individuals with the heterozygous (Hh) and homozygous dominant (HH) genotypes will have the disease, resulting in 75% of the offspring being affected. 100% (choice E) of the offspring are affected when one parent is homozygous for the dominant allele (HH). https://d2vrujxrqm3l5p.cloudfront.net/03763e77-417e-4a5b-9fa9-f0bfc7f62de6.jpg Since only one copy of a dominant mutant allele is necessary for an individual to be affected by an AD disease, then if an affected parent is homozygous dominant, 100% of their offspring will inherit the mutant allele and be affected. A parent can only be homozygous for the dominant mutant allele if he or she was the product of two affected individuals, in which case you would see the mating of two affected individuals diagrammed on a pedigree. As stated previously, in autosomal dominant inheritance patterns, the affected individual is almost always heterozygous. This is due to many factors. First of all, to produce a homozygote, two affected heterozygotes would have to mate. Since autosomal dominant disorders are rare, this is statistically unlikely. Then, even if it does occur, they have only a one in four (25%) chance of even having a homozygous affected child.

In autosomal dominant inheritance, only one copy of a mutant allele is required for an individual to have the disease. When a heterozygous person mates with an unaffected person, there is a one in two (50%) chance with each pregnancy that the offspring will inherit the dominant mutant allele, and therefore, be affected by the disease. Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by an inactivating mutation in the calcium-sensing receptor (CASR). The CASR plays a significant role in the maintenance of serum calcium by regulating parathyroid hormone secretion and urinary calcium excretion.
